# The Chimney-Pots

My windows look across the roofs of the crowded city and my thoughts often take their suggestion from the life that is manifest at my neighbors' windows and on these roofs.

Across the way, one story lower than our own, there dwells "with his subsidiary parents" a little lad who has been ill for several weeks. After his household is up and dressed I regularly discover him in bed, with his books and toys piled about him. Sometimes his knees are raised to form a snowy mountain, and he leads his paper soldiers up the slope. Sometimes his kitten romps across the coverlet and pounces on his wriggling toes; and again sleeps on the sunny window-sill. His book, by his rapt attention, must deal with far-off islands and with waving cocoanut trees. Lately I have observed that a yellow drink is brought to him in the afternoon--a delicious blend of eggs and milk--and by the zest with which he licks the remainder from his lips, it is a prime favorite of his. In these last few days, however, I have seen the lad's nose flat and eager on the window, and I know that he is convalescent.

At another set of windows--now that the days are growing short and there is need of lights--I see in shadowgraph against the curtains an occasional domestic drama. Tonight, by the appearance of hurry and the shifting of garments, I surmise that there is preparation for a party. Presently, when the upstairs lights have disappeared, I shall see these folk below, issuing from their door in glossy raiment. My dear sir and madame, I wish you an agreeable dinner and--if your tooth resembles mine--ice-cream for dessert.

The window of a kitchen, also, is opposite, and I often look on savory messes as they ripen on the fire--a stirring with a long iron spoon. This spoon is of such unusual length that even if one supped with the devil (surely the fearful adage cannot apply to our quiet street) he might lift his food in safety from the common pot.

A good many stories lower there is a bit of roof that is set with wicker furniture and a row of gay plants along the gutter. Here every afternoon exactly at six--the roof being then in shadow--a man appears and reads his evening paper. Later his wife joins him and they eat their supper from a tray. They are sunk almost in a well of buildings which, like the hedge of a fairy garden, shuts them from all contact with the world. And here they sit when the tray has been removed. The twilight falls early at their level and, like cottagers in a valley, they watch the daylight that still gilds the peaks above them.

There is another of these out-of-door rooms above me on a higher building. From my lower level I can see the bright canvas and the side of the trellis that supports it. Here, doubtless, in the cool breeze of these summer evenings, honest folk sip their coffee and watch the lights start across the city.

Thus, all around, I have glimpses of my neighbors--a form against the curtains--a group, in the season, around the fire--the week's darning in a rocker--an early nose sniffing at the open window the morning airs.

But it is these roofs themselves that are the general prospect.

Close at hand are graveled surfaces with spouts and whirling vents and chimneys. Here are posts and lines for washing, and a scuttle from which once a week a laundress pops her head. Although her coming is timed to the very hour--almost to the minute--yet when the scuttle stirs it is with an appearance of mystery, as if one of the forty thieves were below, boosting at the rocks that guard his cave. But the laundress is of so unromantic and jouncing a figure that I abandon the fancy when no more than her shoulders are above the scuttle. She is, however, an amiable creature and, if the wind is right, I hear her singing at her task. When clothespins fill her mouth, she experiments with popular tunes. One of these wooden bipeds once slipped inside and nearly strangled her.

In the distance, on the taller buildings, water tanks are lifted against the sky. They are perched aloft on three fingers, as it were, as if the buildings were just won to prohibition and held up their water cups in the first excitement of a novice to pledge the cause. Let hard liquor crouch and tremble in its rathskeller below the sidewalk! In the basement let musty kegs roll and gurgle with hopeless fear! _Der Tag!_ The roof, the triumphant roof, has gone dry.

This range of buildings with water tanks and towers stops my gaze to the North. There is a crowded world beyond--rolling valleys of humanity--the heights of Harlem--but although my windows stand on tiptoe, they may not discover these distant scenes.

On summer days these roofs burn in the sun and spirals of heat arise. Tar flows from the joints in the tin. Tar and the adder--is it not a bright day that brings them forth? Now washing hangs limp upon the line. There is no frisk in undergarments. These stockings that hang shriveled and anaemic--can it be possible that they once trotted to a lively tune, or that a lifted skirt upon a crosswalk drew the eye? The very spouts and chimneys droop in the heavy sunlight. All the spinning vents are still. On these roofs, as on a steaming altar, August celebrates its hot midsummer rites.

My windows look across the roofs of the crowded city, and my thoughts take their suggestion, oftener than I would care to own, from the life that shows itself at my neighbors' windows and on these roofs. Across the way, one story lower than our own, there dwells "with his subsidiary parents" a little lad who has lain ill these several weeks. His household is up and dressed betimes, yet when I look I regularly discover him still in bed, with his books and toys piled about him. Sometimes he raises his knees beneath the sheet to form a snowy mountain, and leads his paper soldiers up the slope;--a Hannibal of the counterpane. Sometimes his kitten romps across the coverlet and pounces on his wriggling toes; and again it sleeps on the sunny window-sill. He bends over his book with so rapt an attention that it must deal, I think, with far-off islands and waving cocoanut trees. Of late a yellow drink is brought to him in the afternoon (a delicious blend of eggs and milk), and by the zest with which he licks the remainder from his lips I judge it a prime favorite of his. But in these last few days I have seen the lad's nose flat and eager on the window, and a boy's nose does not go to the glass until the fever has gone out of him. He is convalescent.

At another set of windows--now that the days draw in and there is need of lights--I see in shadowgraph against the curtains an occasional domestic drama. Tonight there is a look of hurry, a shifting of garments to and fro, and I surmise that a party is in preparation. Presently the upstairs lights will go out, and I shall see these folk below, issuing from their door in glossy raiment. My dear sir and madame, I wish you an agreeable dinner; and, if your tooth resembles mine, ice-cream for dessert. The window of a kitchen is opposite also, and I often look on savory messes as they ripen on the fire, stirred with a long iron spoon. It is a spoon of such unusual length that a man who supped with the devil (and surely the fearful adage cannot apply to our quiet street) might lift his food in safety from the common pot.

A good many stories lower there is a bit of roof set out with wicker furniture, and a row of gay plants along the gutter. Here every afternoon at six exactly, the roof being then in shadow, a man appears and reads his evening paper. His wife joins him later, and they eat their supper from a tray. They are sunk almost in a well of buildings, which shuts them from all contact with the world as the hedge shuts in a fairy garden; and there they sit on when the tray has been carried off. Twilight comes early at their level. Like cottagers in a valley, they watch the daylight that still gilds the peaks above them. There is another of these out-of-door rooms above me, on a higher building, and from my lower level I can see the bright canvas and the side of the trellis that supports it. Here, doubtless, in the cool breeze of the summer evenings, honest folk sip their coffee and watch the lights start across the city. Thus, all around, I have my glimpses of my neighbors--a form against the curtains; a group, in the season, about the fire; the week's darning in a rocker; an early nose sniffing at the open window the morning airs.

But it is the roofs themselves that make the general prospect. Close at hand are graveled surfaces, with spouts and whirling vents and chimneys; here are posts and lines for washing, and a scuttle from which, once a week, a laundress pops her head. Her coming is timed to the very hour, almost to the minute; and yet when the scuttle stirs, it stirs with an air of mystery, as if one of the forty thieves were below, boosting at the rocks that guard his cave. The fancy does not outlast her shoulders. She is of so unromantic and jouncing a figure that I abandon the cave before more than her shoulders are clear of the scuttle. She is an amiable creature, however, and if the wind sits right I hear her singing at her task. When her mouth is full of clothespins she experiments with popular tunes; and one of these wooden bipeds once slipped inside and nearly strangled her.

In the distance, on the taller buildings, water tanks are lifted against the sky. They are perched aloft on three fingers, as it were, as if the buildings were but newly won to prohibition and held up their water cups, in the first excitement of the novice, to pledge the cause. Let hard liquor crouch and tremble in its rathskeller below the sidewalk! Let the musty kegs roll and gurgle in the basement with a hopeless fear! _Der Tag!_ The roof, the triumphant roof, has gone dry. This range of buildings, with its tanks and towers, stops my gaze to the North. There is a crowded world beyond it--rolling valleys of humanity, and the heights of Harlem--but my windows, though they stand on tiptoe, may not discover these distant scenes.

On summer days these roofs burn in the sun, and spirals of heat go up from them. Tar flows from the joints in the tin. It is the bright day that brings forth the adder, and it brings forth the tar as well. The washing hangs limp upon the line; there is no frisk left in the undergarments. Can it be possible that these stockings, hanging shriveled and anaemic, once trotted to a lively tune, or that a lifted skirt upon a crosswalk ever drew the eye to them? I can scarcely believe it. The very spouts and chimneys droop in the heavy sunlight, and all the spinning vents are still. On these roofs, as on a steaming altar, August celebrates its hot midsummer rites.

candidates.text:
My windows look across the roofs of the crowded city, and I find that my thoughts take their hint, oftener than I would confess, from the life that shows itself at my neighbors' windows and upon these roofs. Across the way, a story below our own, there lives "with his subsidiary parents" a little lad who has been ill these several weeks. When his household is up and dressed I find him still in bed, his books and toys heaped about him like the spoils of a siege. Sometimes he raises his knees and makes a snowy mountain of the coverlet, and leads his paper soldiers up the slope; it is a hard campaign, and the mountain is apt to shift under them. Sometimes his kitten romps across the bed and pounces on his wriggling toes, and at other times it sleeps on the sunny window-sill. He has a book, too, and from the rapt way he bends over it I judge that it deals with far-off islands and waving cocoanut trees. Of late a yellow drink is brought to him in the afternoon (a delicious blend of eggs and milk), and he licks the last of it from his lips with such zest that I set it down as a prime favorite. These last few days, however, I have seen his nose flat and eager on the pane. A boy who looks out of the window like that is mending, and I know that he is convalescent.

At another set of windows, now that the days draw in and the lamps are wanted early, I see an occasional domestic drama played in shadowgraph against the curtains. Tonight there is an appearance of hurry and a shifting of garments, and I surmise a party. Presently the upstairs lights will go out, and I shall see these folk below, issuing from their door in glossy raiment. My dear sir and madame, I wish you an agreeable dinner, and, if your tooth resembles mine, ice-cream to finish it. Opposite, too, is the window of a kitchen, where I often watch savory messes ripening on the fire and being stirred with a long iron spoon. The spoon is of such uncommon length that a man who supped with the devil might lift his food from the common pot in perfect safety; though I am sure the fearful adage has nothing to do with our quiet street.

A good many stories lower lies a bit of roof set out with wicker furniture, and a row of gay plants along the gutter. Every afternoon at six exactly, when the roof has fallen into shadow, a man comes out and reads his evening paper. His wife joins him later, and they eat their supper from a tray. They are sunk almost in a well of buildings, which shut them from all contact with the world as the hedge shuts in a fairy garden; and there they sit on, after the tray is carried off. Twilight comes early at their level. They watch the daylight that still gilds the peaks above them, like cottagers in a valley. There is another of these out-of-door rooms above me, on a higher building, and from my lower level I can make out its bright canvas and the side of the trellis that holds it up. Here, doubtless, in the cool breeze of the summer evenings, honest folk sip their coffee and watch the lights start across the city. So on every side I have my glimpses of my neighbors:--a form against the curtains--a group about the fire, in its season--the week's darning left in a rocker--an early nose sniffing the morning airs at the open window.

Yet it is the roofs themselves that make the general prospect. Close at hand are graveled surfaces, with spouts and whirling vents and chimneys; here are posts and lines for washing, and a scuttle out of which a laundress pops her head once a week. Her coming is timed to the hour, almost to the minute. Nevertheless, when the scuttle stirs there is a kind of mystery in it, as if one of the forty thieves were below, boosting at the rocks that guard his cave. But the laundress is so unromantic and jouncing a figure that I give up the fancy before her shoulders are fairly above the scuttle. She is an amiable creature, for all that, and when the wind sets right I hear her singing at her work. She tries over the popular tunes with her mouth full of clothespins. One of these wooden bipeds slipped inside once, and nearly strangled her.

In the distance, on the taller buildings, the water tanks are lifted against the sky. Each stands perched aloft on three fingers, as it were, as though the buildings had just been won to prohibition and held up their water cups, in the first fervor of the convert, to pledge the cause. Let hard liquor crouch and tremble in its rathskeller below the sidewalk! Let the musty kegs roll and gurgle in the basement with hopeless fear! _Der Tag!_ The roof, the triumphant roof, has gone dry. This range of tanks and towers stops my gaze to the North. Beyond it lies a crowded world, rolling valleys of humanity and the heights of Harlem; but my windows may stand on tiptoe as they please, they shall not discover these distant scenes.

On summer days these roofs burn in the sun, and spirals of heat go up from them. The tar flows out of the joints in the tin; it is the bright day that brings forth the tar and the adder. The washing hangs limp upon the line. There is no frisk left in the undergarments. These stockings, shriveled and anaemic as they hang, once trotted to a lively tune, I suppose, and drew the eye from under a lifted skirt upon a crosswalk; I can scarcely believe it now. The very spouts and chimneys droop in the heavy light, and the spinning vents are still. On these roofs, as on a steaming altar, August celebrates its hot midsummer rites.

My windows look across the roofs of the crowded city, and my thoughts often take their suggestion from the life I see at my neighbors' windows and on these roofs. Across the way, one story lower than our own, there dwells "with his subsidiary parents" a little lad who has been ill for several weeks. After his household is up and dressed I regularly discover him still in bed, with his books and toys piled about him. Sometimes he raises his knees to form a snowy mountain and leads his paper soldiers up the slope. He has a kitten, too; sometimes it romps across the coverlet and pounces on his wriggling toes, and sometimes it sleeps on the sunny window-sill. His book, if I judge by his rapt attention, must deal with far-off islands and waving cocoanut trees. Lately I have seen a yellow drink brought to him in the afternoon (a delicious blend of eggs and milk), and by the zest with which he licks the last of it from his lips it is a prime favorite of his. In these few days past, however, I have seen his nose flat and eager on the window. A boy who presses his nose to the glass is on the mend, and I know that he is convalescent.

At another set of windows, now that the days are growing short and there is need of lights, I see in shadowgraph against the curtains an occasional domestic drama. Tonight there is an appearance of hurry and a shifting of garments, and I surmise a party. Presently, when the upstairs lights have gone out, I shall see these folk issue from their door below in glossy raiment. My dear sir and madame, I wish you an agreeable dinner, and, if your tooth resembles mine, ice-cream for dessert! The window of a kitchen is opposite also, and I often look on savory messes as they ripen on the fire, stirred with a long iron spoon. The spoon is of such unusual length that even if one supped with the devil (and surely the fearful adage cannot apply to our quiet street) he might lift his food in safety from the common pot.

A good many stories lower there is a bit of roof set with wicker furniture, with a row of gay plants along the gutter. Here every afternoon at exactly six, when the roof lies in shadow, a man appears and reads his evening paper. Later his wife joins him, and they eat their supper from a tray. They are sunk almost in a well of buildings, which shuts them from all contact with the world like the hedge of a fairy garden; and there they sit on when the tray has been taken away. The twilight falls early at their level. Like cottagers in a valley, they watch the daylight that still gilds the peaks above them. There is another of these out-of-door rooms above me, on a higher building, and from my lower level I can see its bright canvas and the side of the trellis that holds it up. Here, doubtless, in the cool breeze of these summer evenings, honest folk sip their coffee and watch the lights start across the city. So on every side I have glimpses of my neighbors:--a form against the curtains; a group, in the season, around the fire; the week's darning in a rocker; an early nose at the open window, sniffing the morning airs.

But it is these roofs themselves that make the general prospect. Close at hand are graveled surfaces with spouts, whirling vents and chimneys. Here are posts and lines for washing, and a scuttle from which a laundress pops her head once a week. Her coming is timed to the very hour, almost to the minute; yet when the scuttle stirs it is with an air of mystery, as if one of the forty thieves were below, boosting at the rocks that guard his cave. But she is of so unromantic and jouncing a figure that I give up the fancy before more than her shoulders are above the scuttle. She is an amiable creature, however. If the wind is right I hear her singing at her task, and when her mouth is full of clothespins she experiments with popular tunes. One of these wooden bipeds once slipped inside and nearly strangled her.

In the distance, on the taller buildings, water tanks are lifted against the sky. They stand aloft on three fingers, as it were, as if the buildings had just been won to prohibition and held up their water cups, in the first excitement of the novice, to pledge the cause. Let hard liquor crouch and tremble in its rathskeller below the sidewalk! Let the musty kegs roll and gurgle in the basement with hopeless fear! _Der Tag!_ The roof, the triumphant roof, has gone dry. This range of buildings, with its water tanks and towers, stops my gaze to the North. There is a crowded world beyond it, rolling valleys of humanity and the heights of Harlem; but though my windows stand on tiptoe, they may not discover these distant scenes.

On summer days these roofs burn in the sun, and spirals of heat go up from them. Tar flows from the joints in the tin. Tar and the adder--is it not a bright day that brings them forth? It is; and on such a day the washing hangs limp upon the line, and there is no frisk left in the undergarments. These stockings hang shriveled and anaemic. Can it be possible that they once trotted to a lively tune, or that a lifted skirt upon a crosswalk drew the eye? It hardly seems so now. The very spouts and chimneys droop in the heavy sunlight, and all the spinning vents are still. On these roofs, as on a steaming altar, August celebrates its hot midsummer rites.
